country.comment: The primary empirical analysis studies urban and peri-urban Zambia. In selecting the case-study country, the authors also conducted a preliminary secondary data availability audit across all 54 African Union member states (shortlisting 5 countries with user, provider, and regulator availability metrics).
country.where_found: PDF Page 1, Title & Abstract; PDF Pages 3–5, Materials and methods ('Study country selection' and 'Study site'); Fig 1, PDF Page 4

effect_estimate.comment: Weighted descriptive prevalence of >=1 full-day interruption in the prior fortnight is reported as 47% (95% CI: 45%, 49% in Abstract; 47%, 95% CI: 44%, 49% on PDF p. 9; 46.7% weighted / n = 1,398 of 3,047 unweighted in Table 1). Provider-level non-revenue water and continuity (hrs/day) were significantly associated with user-reported interruptions in bivariate chi-square tests (p < 0.001, Table 2) but excluded via backward elimination or collinearity screening in final multivariable multilevel models.
effect_estimate.value: Overall, 46.7% (n = 1,398/3,047; reported as 47%, 95% CI: 44%–49% in text and 45%–49% in Abstract) of urban and peri-urban piped-water households reported water unavailability for >=1 full day in the preceding two weeks, varying across the 11 regulated Water and Sewerage Company (WSC) provider coverage areas from 18.7% (reported as 19%, 95% CI: 15%–24% in text; 18%, 95% CI: 14%–23% in Abstract) in Lukanga WSC to 77.0% (reported as 77%, 95% CI: 71%–82% in text; 76%, 95% CI: 70%–81% in Abstract) in Kafubu WSC. In two-level multilevel logistic regression (n = 3,047 households in 177 clusters), home ownership/tenure (at least partly owning vs not owning home) was associated with higher odds of interruption in Model 1 (OR = 1.31, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01) and Model 2 (OR = 1.32, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01). Controlling for household factors (Model 1, ref: Lusaka WSC), odds of interruption differed markedly by WSC service area: Lukanga WSC OR = 0.36 (SE = 0.15, p < 0.05), Nkana WSC OR = 2.24 (SE = 0.90, p < 0.10), Chambeshi WSC OR = 2.43 (SE = 0.94, p < 0.05), Luapula WSC OR = 2.89 (SE = 1.45, p < 0.05), Mulongo WSC OR = 3.77 (SE = 1.85, p < 0.05), and Kafubu WSC OR = 8.02 (SE = 3.40, p < 0.01). In Model 2, using a neighbour's piped tap vs piped into dwelling had OR = 1.33 (SE = 0.21, p < 0.10); provider-level GDP per capita per $1,000 increase had OR = 0.51 (SE = 0.11, p < 0.01); regulator-reported LPCD main effect was OR = 1.01 (SE = 0.01, ns), interacting with middle neighbourhood wealth (OR = 0.97, SE = 0.01, p < 0.05) and provider GDP per capita (OR = 1.02, SE = 0.01, p < 0.01).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational cross-sectional analysis appraised with JBI (design ceiling = 2). Assigned 1 (documented statistical association) because the study quantifies cross-sectional statistical associations between housing tenure (home ownership), statutory utility provider coverage areas, and regulatory supply metrics with household-reported service interruptions, without directly observing administrative or legal decision-making mechanisms.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF Pages 7–9, Materials and methods; PDF Pages 14–17, Results & Discussion; Table 4 (PDF Page 15)

mechanism_flags.comment: Housing tenure / home ownership ('Home ownership', referred to as 'tenure' in S13 Table) and statutory utility provider coverage areas ('service_area' boundaries of the 11 NWASCO-regulated commercial WSCs, with rural areas excluded from utility/regulator scope) are directly modeled as explanatory variables for water service interruptions.
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF Pages 5–8, Materials and methods; Table 1 (PDF Page 11); Table 3 (PDF Page 13); Table 4 (PDF Page 15); S13 Table caption (PDF Page 21)

outcome_flags.comment: Primary outcome is household-reported piped drinking-water service continuity/reliability (>=1 full day of interruption in the past two weeks), compared and modeled alongside utility- and regulator-reported continuity (average service hours/day), residential water quantity supplied/consumed (LPCD vs WHO 50 LPCD benchmark), and piped drinking-water access when needed (SDG 6.1.1 availability criterion across dwelling, yard/standpipe, and neighbour tap connections).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF Page 2, Introduction; PDF Pages 5–8, Materials and methods ('Data sources and availability metrics' and 'Outcome and explanatory variables'); PDF Page 9, Results

sample_size.comment: From the 2018 Zambia DHS, 8,117 rural households (347 clusters), 47 households with missing GPS (2 clusters), 1,574 non-piped water households, and 46 'don't know' responses were excluded (Fig 2), leaving n = 3,047 urban/peri-urban piped-water households in 177 clusters across all 11 WSCs.
sample_size.value: 3,047 urban and peri-urban households nested in 177 DHS household clusters across 11 commercial Water and Sewerage Companies (provider coverage areas); 54 African Union member states audited in preliminary country selection
sample_size.where_found: PDF Page 1, Abstract; Fig 1 (PDF Page 4); PDF Pages 5–7 & Fig 2 (PDF Page 6); PDF Pages 9–10; Table 4 (PDF Page 15)

study_design.comment: Observational cross-sectional design combining cluster-georeferenced 2018 DHS household survey data with utility (IBNET) and statutory regulator (NWASCO) indicators via Pearson/Spearman correlations, weighted chi-square tests, and unweighted two-level random-intercept logistic regression models.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional study spatially linking nationally representative multi-stage cluster household survey data (2018 Zambia DHS) with utility database (2017 IBNET) and regulator report (2018 NWASCO) records, analyzed using weighted bivariate statistics and two-level multilevel logistic regression
study_design.where_found: PDF Page 1, Title & Abstract; PDF Pages 3–9, Materials and methods; Table 4 (PDF Page 15)
